# "We Did Not Adapt and Move Quickly Enough": What IBM's Earnings Miss Says About Enterprise AI Spending

## The Real Story Isn't the Stock Drop

IBM's stock took a hit after the company issued a preliminary Q2 earnings update that fell short of expectations. But the headline number isn't what matters here. The real signal is what this miss reveals about how enterprise AI spending is actually playing out — and it's not matching the narrative.

When a company the size of IBM stumbles and points to AI infrastructure as a key factor, it's worth paying attention. Not because IBM is the bellwether it once was, but because their missteps tend to reflect broader market realities that smaller players will hit six months later.

## What Actually Happened

IBM released preliminary second-quarter earnings that came in below analyst expectations, triggering a significant drop in share value. The company acknowledged it had not moved quickly enough to capture AI infrastructure opportunities.

According to reporting from The New Stack, the earnings miss is tied directly to IBM's positioning in the AI infrastructure market. The company has been working to reposition itself as an AI-first enterprise vendor, but the results suggest that strategy isn't translating to revenue at the pace investors expected.

The phrase that keeps surfacing in coverage: "We did not adapt and move quickly enough."

That's a remarkably candid admission from a company of IBM's stature. It's also a phrase that should resonate with anyone working in enterprise technology. Adaptation speed has become the differentiator — not just for startups, but for legacy players trying to stay relevant.

IBM's AI story has centered on watsonx, their enterprise AI and data platform. The pitch has been about bringing generative AI capabilities to enterprises that need governance, security, and integration with existing infrastructure. On paper, it's exactly what large organizations should want. In practice, the revenue isn't materializing fast enough.

## The Broader Pattern: AI Infrastructure Spending Is Lumpy

IBM's miss isn't happening in isolation. Enterprise AI spending is proving harder to predict than the hype cycle suggested.

Here's what the market expected: Organizations would rush to deploy AI infrastructure, creating a steady wave of spending that lifted all boats — hardware vendors, cloud providers, consulting firms, and platform companies like IBM.

Here's what's actually happening: Spending is concentrated. A handful of hyperscalers and chip companies are capturing most of the infrastructure dollars. Enterprises are experimenting with AI but not committing to the long-term platform investments that generate recurring revenue.

The gap between "we're exploring AI" and "we're committing budget to AI infrastructure" is wider than vendor roadshows would have you believe.

For IBM specifically, the challenge is twofold. First, they're competing for AI infrastructure dollars against cloud providers who already own the compute relationship. Second, enterprises are still figuring out which AI investments actually produce ROI — and that uncertainty delays big platform commitments.

The New Stack's coverage highlights that IBM's AI infrastructure play requires enterprises to make significant architectural decisions. Those decisions are slow. They involve procurement cycles, security reviews, compliance assessments, and stakeholder alignment. By the time an enterprise is ready to commit, the market may have moved again.

## Why Practitioners Should Care

If you're building software and thinking about AI integrations, IBM's earnings miss tells you something important: the enterprise market is still in discovery mode.

That has practical implications for how you plan.

**Your AI vendors might not be around in the same form in 18 months.** The AI infrastructure market is going through rapid consolidation and repositioning. Companies that seem like safe enterprise bets today are scrambling to adapt. IBM is one of the most stable players in enterprise technology, and they're publicly admitting they moved too slowly. Smaller vendors are under even more pressure.

**"AI-ready" enterprise platforms are not all equivalent.** The market is flooded with AI positioning. Every enterprise vendor has an AI story. But the substance behind those stories varies wildly. IBM's watsonx is a real platform with real capabilities. The problem isn't whether the technology works — it's whether enterprises are ready to adopt it at scale. That readiness gap affects everyone selling into the enterprise.

**Procurement cycles for AI infrastructure are longer than vendor timelines.** If you're building tooling that depends on a specific AI platform being in place, factor in the reality that enterprise adoption is measured in quarters or years, not weeks. The gap between a pilot and production deployment is where most AI initiatives stall.

**Your security and compliance requirements add friction.** One reason enterprise AI spending is lumpy is that organizations with mature security programs move cautiously. They're asking hard questions about data residency, model governance, access controls, and audit trails. Those questions slow down adoption — which is probably appropriate, but it also means vendor revenue projections based on rapid adoption are frequently wrong.

## The Adaptation Problem Is Real

IBM's admission that they didn't adapt quickly enough isn't just corporate spin for a bad quarter. It reflects a genuine challenge that affects the entire enterprise AI market.

The technology is moving faster than enterprise procurement. Generative AI capabilities that seemed cutting-edge 12 months ago are now table stakes. Enterprises that started AI initiatives in early 2023 are finding that their initial assumptions about tooling and platforms are already outdated.

This creates a weird dynamic. Enterprises delay decisions because the market is changing too fast. But the delay itself becomes a competitive disadvantage. And vendors like IBM get caught in the middle — unable to close deals because customers are waiting, but also falling behind because they're trying to serve a market that hasn't fully committed.

For practitioners inside enterprises, this adaptation gap shows up in frustrating ways. Your AI pilot might work, but scaling it requires platform decisions that leadership keeps deferring. Or you've built tooling around one vendor's API, and now there's internal pressure to evaluate three alternatives. Or your security team is still working through the governance framework for AI models, blocking production deployment.

None of this is unique to IBM's situation. But IBM's earnings miss makes the problem visible in a way that internal planning discussions don't.

## The Competitive Landscape Is Shifting

IBM's stumble is happening while other players are capturing AI infrastructure dollars. The hyperscalers — AWS, Azure, and GCP — are all reporting strong AI-related revenue growth [UNVERIFIED — specific growth numbers would need verification against each company's earnings]. Nvidia's datacenter revenue continues to surge on the back of AI chip demand.

The pattern suggests that enterprises are spending on AI infrastructure, but they're spending it with cloud providers and hardware vendors rather than platform companies like IBM.

This makes sense if you think about how enterprises actually adopt new technology. They start with what they already have. If you're an Azure shop, your first AI experiments happen on Azure. If you're running AWS, you're using Bedrock and SageMaker. The multi-cloud, platform-agnostic AI infrastructure play is a harder sell because it requires a new relationship and new architectural decisions.

IBM's pitch — enterprise-grade AI with governance and security built in — is compelling on paper. But it requires enterprises to make IBM a strategic partner for AI, not just use AI features from their existing cloud provider. That's a different sale, and it's a longer one.

## What to Watch

**IBM's next earnings call.** The preliminary numbers triggered the stock drop, but the full earnings report will include more detail about where AI revenue is actually coming from and what the pipeline looks like. Pay attention to whether they adjust their positioning or timeline.

**Enterprise AI adoption surveys.** Multiple analyst firms track enterprise AI spending intentions. If IBM's miss reflects broader hesitation, it should show up in those surveys over the next few quarters. Look for gaps between "planning to invest" and "have allocated budget."

**Hyperscaler AI revenue.** Compare IBM's results against AWS, Azure, and GCP AI revenue disclosures. If the hyperscalers are growing while IBM stalls, that tells you where the market is actually moving.

**Your own vendor conversations.** If you're in procurement discussions with AI platform vendors, notice the pressure. Are vendors pushing harder for commitments? Are they offering more aggressive pricing? Are they pivoting their messaging? Desperation shows up in sales conversations before it shows up in earnings reports.

## What to Do

If you're responsible for AI-related decisions on your team, IBM's earnings miss is a data point worth incorporating into your planning.

**Don't overcommit to platforms that might reposition.** The AI infrastructure market is volatile. Long-term contracts with vendors who are struggling to find their footing carry risk. Build in flexibility where you can.

**Validate your vendor's financial stability.** This doesn't mean IBM is going anywhere — they're not. But smaller AI vendors are under pressure. If you're depending on a startup's AI tooling, pay attention to their funding runway and market position.

**Factor in enterprise adoption timelines when building tooling.** If you're building internal tooling that depends on specific AI platforms, assume the adoption timeline will be longer than vendor projections suggest. Build for portability where practical.

**Document your AI architecture decisions.** In a fast-moving market, being able to explain why you made specific platform choices — and what would trigger a reevaluation — is valuable. When leadership asks why you picked vendor X, you want an answer that references your actual requirements, not just their marketing pitch.

## The Open Question

IBM's admission that they didn't adapt quickly enough raises a question that applies beyond their specific situation:

**In a market where the technology changes faster than enterprise procurement cycles, how do you make platform decisions that won't be obsolete by the time they're implemented?**

I don't have a clean answer. The standard advice — build for abstraction, avoid lock-in, stay flexible — is easier to say than to execute. Real systems have real dependencies. Moving fast sometimes means committing before the market stabilizes.

But IBM's earnings miss is a reminder that even large, well-resourced companies are getting this wrong. If they can't adapt quickly enough, what does that mean for the rest of us?
